title: Valmont Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Valmont wells have a 35 ft median depth, with fractured bedrock and finished-well costs modeled at $8,300-$15,500.
intro_html:
Buying land near Valmont means looking past the presence of a well permit. The records within 5 miles show a wide range of conditions, from shallow wells in local alluvium to much deeper wells in fractured mountain bedrock. The median reported depth is 35 feet, but the middle half runs from 20 to 200 feet.

That spread matters when you compare a property, request a drilling estimate, or plan a new home. Reported yields are generally useful, but the records are not complete: 4,001 wells report total depth, while only 568 report a pump yield and 174 report a static water level. Use this guide as local screening information, then verify the specific parcel with Colorado DWR records, a driller, and the county requirements.

sections.heading: Valmont well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
Valmont’s reported well depths are unusually spread out for a mountain-area setting. The median is 35 feet, and the middle half falls between 20 and 200 feet. About 65% of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 21% fall from 100 to 300 feet and 14% from 300 to 600 feet. One percent are 600 feet or deeper, with the deepest record reaching 3,000 feet.

The local geology helps explain the uncertainty. Permits most often name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 4,917 wells in that category. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water through cracks rather than through a uniform layer, so two nearby lots may not drill alike. A driller’s bid should state the assumed depth, casing and grout work, and what happens if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: What a Valmont well may produce
sections.html:
Among the 568 records that report a pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 7.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 63% fall in the 5 to 15 gallons-per-minute range, and 27% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Eight percent are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a useful local benchmark, not a promise for a particular lot. A yield test, storage tank, and pump setup determine how comfortably a home can use the water during peak demand. An exempt household-use well also has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Ask for the well construction report and pumping information instead of relying on a seller’s verbal description.

sections.heading: Valmont water levels look shallow, without a simple decline
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are shallow in this area. The median depth to water is 10 feet, and the middle half is 6 to 20 feet below the surface. That can reduce lift for a pump, but it also means groundwater and surface activities deserve attention during site planning.

The decade figures do not show a steady downward trend. Median measurements were 16 feet in the 1950s, 25 in the 1960s, 22 in the 1970s, 6 in the 2000s, 9 in the 2010s, and 9 in the 2020s. Measurements come from different wells and dates, so they are a regional reference rather than a water-table guarantee for your parcel. Confirm the current static level and seasonal behavior on the property.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Valmont
sections.html:
Permit activity stretches across several generations. The records show 279 permits from the 1950s, 266 from the 1960s, 578 from the 1970s, 451 from the 1980s, 921 from the 1990s, 631 from the 2000s, 604 from the 2010s, and 543 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Those records cover domestic and household use most often, at 48%. Monitoring wells account for 33%, while stock and irrigation make up 3% and 2%. The most active named drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Waneka & Son Drilling, and Ground Water Systems Inc. A permit is not the same as a completed, productive well, so check construction records and the permit’s permitted use before treating it as evidence for a home site.

sections.heading: Valmont well drilling cost: a useful planning range
sections.html:
For Valmont’s fractured mountain bedrock, the cost model uses a drilling rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $2,300-$3,500. That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical models to about $8,300-$15,500.

Depth is only one part of the bid. Casing, grout, access for the rig, difficult rock, water testing, and the final pump arrangement can change the total. The local depth distribution is the reason not to budget from the median alone: the middle half extends to 200 feet, and some records are far deeper. Get a written estimate that separates drilling from completion and states the assumptions.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying near Valmont
sections.html:
Environmental screening deserves more than a quick visual inspection. Within about 10 miles, the mapped data include 346 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 460 historic mine features, and 63 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those figures do not prove a problem at a particular address, but they support testing and a review of nearby land uses, drainage, and historic activity.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock, even where nearby wells perform well. Test existing water for appropriate contaminants and inspect the wellhead, casing, grout, pressure tank, and treatment equipment. Septic setbacks, replacement areas, access for drilling, and the location of a future house can be just as important as the well itself. Confirm requirements with Boulder County and Colorado DWR before closing or building.

sections.heading: A practical Valmont lot-checking plan
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a broad map point. Review nearby permits toward Boulder, Gunbarrel, Paragon Estates, Niwot, Pine Brook Hill, and Leyner, then compare reported depth, yield, aquifer name, use, and construction status. The 30% share of wells identified with Denver Basin aquifers is another reason to confirm the actual aquifer and permit conditions for the lot.

For an existing home, request the well permit, construction report, recent production information, water-quality results, and service history. For vacant land, have a licensed driller evaluate access and likely depth before setting a house or septic layout. Water rights can also control what a well may legally supply; over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan. Price the well, septic system, driveway, power, and site work together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Valmont, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Valmont is 35 feet. The middle half runs from 20 to 200 feet. About 65% are under 100 feet, but 14% are from 300 to 600 feet and the deepest record is 3,000 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make the exact depth parcel-specific.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Valmont?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to $2,300-$3,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical models to $8,300-$15,500. A written bid should identify depth assumptions, casing, grout, access, and completion work.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Valmont?
faq.a: Of the Valmont-area records reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 7.0-15.0. About 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 27% report more than 15. These are regional records, not a guarantee. Require a yield test and review storage and pump capacity.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Valmont, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a nearby well’s yield. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 346 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 460 historic mine features, and 63 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water and review nearby land uses. Septic systems, mine history, and local drainage should be part of the review.

Yes, reported static water levels are relatively shallow: the median is 10 feet below the surface, with a middle half of 6 to 20 feet. Decade medians range from 6 feet in the 2000s to 25 feet in the 1960s, so the series does not show a simple steady decline. A parcel-specific measurement is still necessary.
